# OpenPilot + Core RL Master Context

This is the master context for the whole learning thread so far.

The goal is not to create a shallow portfolio page. The goal is to build a serious end-to-end project and learning track that presents strong engineering judgment for self-driving companies, especially comma.ai-style engineering, with reinforcement learning as the primary research skill.

The current identity we are building toward is:

> RL-first autonomous driving engineer who understands the deployed AV stack, can read real production code, can formalize control problems as RL problems, and can run disciplined experiments.

## Current North Star

The project direction is:

```text
OpenPilot system understanding
  -> model-side code literacy
  -> control boundary understanding
  -> core RL fundamentals
  -> PPO from first principles
  -> PufferLib training stack
  -> comma controls challenge experiments
  -> research-style writeup and reproducible results
```

The important rule:

```text
concept first
equation / pseudocode second
repo code third
notes update last
```

This rule exists because file lists alone do not teach the system. We need to understand what each part is doing, why it exists, what assumptions it makes, and how it can fail.

## What Started This

The first workspace context was an end-to-end driving project under `version-beta`, with notes, source code, checkpoints, and data folders. That project was not tracked by its own Git repo. The only Git repos on disk were dependency clones such as OpenPilot, Waymax, tinygrad, PufferDrive, CARLA-related folders, and other dependencies.

The first stated goal was to present engineering ability to self-driving car companies and startups. The strongest stated interest was comma.ai and reinforcement learning with PufferLib.

That created two parallel needs:

1. Learn the OpenPilot ecosystem properly, not superficially.
2. Build RL depth that can later become an applied AV control project.

## Shift Away From Portfolio Thinking

The project should not be described as only a portfolio.

A portfolio usually says:

```text
here are finished artifacts
```

This project should say:

```text
here is a serious engineering/research process:
  I read production AV code,
  I formalized problems,
  I built baselines,
  I trained agents,
  I evaluated failure modes,
  I documented tradeoffs.
```

That difference matters. Self-driving teams care about judgment, debugging, evaluation discipline, and the ability to understand complex systems.

## OpenPilot Repo Walkthrough: What We Chose To Focus On

The first requested repo was:

[commaai/openpilot](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot)

The user asked to clone it, open it in VS Code, and walk through code one file at a time. The first attempt felt like a dump because it listed many files without enough algorithmic explanation.

The corrected approach became:

```text
do not start with every process
do not start with car wiring
do not start with CAN / OBD
start with the model path
```

So the OpenPilot learning focus became:

1. camera image input
2. image preprocessing
3. virtual camera warp
4. YUV / NV12 input format
5. ONNX model contract
6. temporal inputs
7. model outputs
8. parsing model predictions
9. turning plan into action
10. understanding where controls begin

We intentionally postponed:

1. OBD details
2. CAN message plumbing
3. full daemon/process architecture
4. hardware setup
5. car-specific integration

This was a deliberate scope choice, not an omission.

## OpenPilot Model Mental Model

The high-level model path is:

```text
camera frame
  -> real camera image buffer
  -> virtual model-camera warp
  -> YUV / NV12 handling
  -> packed model tensor
  -> ONNX / compiled model execution
  -> raw model outputs
  -> parsed predictions
  -> plan
  -> desired curvature / desired acceleration
  -> controls boundary
```

The model is not simply:

```text
picture -> steering
```

It is closer to:

```text
recent camera views
+ compact temporal memory
+ desire / navigation context
+ traffic-side convention
+ previous action context
  -> predicted future scene and ego motion
  -> plan and action-relevant outputs
```

That distinction matters. The model is doing prediction and planning-like output, not only direct joystick control.

## The Model Inputs

The deployed model contract includes multiple inputs.

The important ones we discussed:

```text
img
big_img
features_buffer
desire_pulse
traffic_convention
action_t
```

Reference:

[OpenPilot model README](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/models/README.md)

The beginner explanation:

```text
img:
  recent model-camera visual stream

big_img:
  recent wide/big visual stream

features_buffer:
  learned temporal memory from previous model runs

desire_pulse:
  short signal for desired maneuver, such as lane change intent

traffic_convention:
  left-hand vs right-hand traffic context

action_t:
  previous action/context input used by the temporal policy
```

## `img` And `big_img`

The confusing part was `big_img`.

The key correction:

```text
big_img does not simply mean the tensor is bigger.
```

In the exported model contract we looked at, both `img` and `big_img` can have the same tensor shape:

```text
img      = (1, 12, 128, 256)
big_img  = (1, 12, 128, 256)
```

The difference is conceptual/source-level:

```text
img:
  normal model view

big_img:
  wider / alternate visual stream processed into the same model tensor shape
```

So `big_img` means:

```text
another visual stream, not necessarily a larger array at inference time
```

## Why 12 Channels

The model uses two recent frames.

Each frame is packed into 6 YUV-derived channels.

So:

```text
6 channels per frame * 2 frames = 12 channels
```

The beginner version:

```text
one model frame:
  YUV information packed into 6 channels

two recent model frames:
  12 total channels
```

The model does not receive a normal RGB image like:

```text
height x width x 3
```

It receives a packed video-camera-friendly representation that is efficient for the runtime system and aligned with training.

## YUV

YUV is a way to represent image information.

It separates:

```text
Y = brightness / luma
U = blue-ish color difference / chroma
V = red-ish color difference / chroma
```

The simple version:

```text
Y tells how bright the pixel is.
U and V tell color information.
```

This is common in camera and video systems because human vision is more sensitive to brightness detail than color detail. That means brightness can be stored at higher resolution and color can often be stored more compactly.

## NV12

NV12 is not a different color scale from YUV.

The distinction is:

```text
YUV = what the numbers mean
NV12 = how the YUV numbers are arranged in memory
```

NV12 stores:

```text
Y plane:
  brightness for every pixel

UV plane:
  lower-resolution color data, with U and V interleaved
```

Memory layout:

```text
YYYYYYYYYYYY...
UVUVUVUVUV...
```

So when OpenPilot receives camera frames in an NV12-like format, it must treat brightness and color planes correctly before packing the model input.

## Planes, Not Driving Plans

There was a naming confusion around "plane."

In image processing:

```text
Y plane = brightness image
U plane = color component image
V plane = color component image
```

This is unrelated to a driving plan.

In model output:

```text
plan = predicted future ego motion / path-like output
```

So:

```text
image plane:
  one layer of image data

driving plan:
  model output about future motion
```

## Real Camera vs Virtual Model Camera

This was one of the most important concepts.

There is one real physical camera view coming from the device. But the model was trained expecting images that look like they came from a consistent virtual camera geometry.

So OpenPilot does:

```text
real camera image
  -> warp into virtual model camera view
```

The virtual camera is not another physical sensor. It is a coordinate convention.

The point is to make the model see a stable view even if real camera calibration, mounting, or lens parameters differ slightly.

## Camera Intrinsics

Camera intrinsics describe how 3D rays project into 2D pixels.

Important terms:

```text
focal length:
  how zoomed-in or wide the camera projection is

center point:
  where the optical center lands in the image
```

The center point is measured in pixel coordinates inside the image.

If the image coordinate system is:

```text
x grows left to right
y grows top to bottom
```

then the center point is usually around:

```text
(image_width / 2, image_height / 2)
```

unless the camera calibration says the optical center is slightly shifted.

In OpenPilot model geometry constants, names like `MEDMODEL_CY` and `medmodel_fl` refer to this virtual model camera projection:

```text
MEDMODEL_CY:
  vertical center coordinate of the model camera

medmodel_fl:
  model camera focal length
```

## Warp Matrix

The warp matrix is a 3x3 coordinate translator.

It answers:

```text
for a pixel location in one image view,
where is the corresponding location in another image view?
```

For the model preprocessing path, it is used to connect:

```text
real camera geometry
+ calibration
+ virtual model camera geometry
= mapping between camera image and model image
```

Reference:

[get_warp_matrix](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/common/transformations/model.py#L64)

The conceptual formula:

```text
warp_matrix = camera_from_calib @ calib_from_model
```

Plain English:

```text
start in model-camera coordinates
convert through calibrated road/device geometry
end in real camera pixel coordinates
```

## Perspective Warp Coordinates

A 3x3 perspective warp takes an output pixel coordinate:

```text
(x, y)
```

turns it into homogeneous coordinates:

```text
[x, y, 1]
```

multiplies by the matrix:

```text
[sx, sy, sw] = M * [x, y, 1]
```

then divides:

```text
source_x = sx / sw
source_y = sy / sw
```

The division by `sw` is what allows perspective effects. It is more general than a simple shift, scale, or rotation.

## Why Reverse Mapping

This was the hardest concept and needed several re-explanations.

The key naming correction:

```text
output image = output of the warp operation
```

It does not mean:

```text
neural network output
```

The warped image is created before the neural network runs.

The preprocessing sequence is:

```text
real camera image
  -> warp operation
  -> warped output image
  -> neural network input
  -> neural network output
```

Reverse mapping means:

```text
for every pixel in the model-ready output image:
  ask where it should come from in the real camera image
  sample that source pixel
  write it into this output pixel
```

Pseudocode:

```text
for y_out in output_height:
  for x_out in output_width:
    x_src, y_src = inverse_warp(x_out, y_out)
    output[y_out, x_out] = sample(input, x_src, y_src)
```

Forward mapping would do:

```text
for every pixel in the real camera image:
  compute where it lands in the model image
  write it there
```

The problem with forward mapping is that transformed coordinates usually land between integer pixels. Some output pixels may receive no source pixel. Some may receive multiple source pixels. That creates holes and collision choices.

Reverse mapping avoids the hole problem because it visits every output pixel exactly once. Each model-ready output pixel asks for its source.

Important nuance:

```text
reverse mapping does not mean every source pixel is used exactly once
```

If the warp compresses an area, multiple output pixels can sample nearby or even the same source pixel. If the warp stretches an area, interpolation/nearest-neighbor choices estimate missing detail. But every output pixel gets assigned.

## Sampling Estimate

The warp matrix computes continuous coordinates.

Example:

```text
output pixel (100, 50)
  -> source coordinate (432.7, 211.2)
```

Images live on an integer grid:

```text
(432, 211)
(433, 211)
(432, 212)
(433, 212)
```

So the warp must estimate the sampled value.

Common methods:

```text
nearest neighbor:
  choose the closest integer pixel

bilinear:
  blend the four surrounding pixels
```

The OpenPilot tinygrad warp path we studied uses nearest-neighbor-style sampling in this preprocessing path.

Reference:

[warp_perspective_tinygrad](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/compile_modeld.py#L50)

## Warping Y, U, And V

The warp is done plane by plane.

It is not:

```text
warp the abstract idea of an image once
```

It is:

```text
real Y plane -> warped Y plane
real U plane -> warped U plane
real V plane -> warped V plane
```

Then those warped planes are packed into the model tensor.

Reference anchors:

1. [warp Y](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/compile_modeld.py#L103)
2. [warp U](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/compile_modeld.py#L106)
3. [warp V](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/compile_modeld.py#L109)
4. [join YUV and pack tensor](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/compile_modeld.py#L112)

The full preprocessing chain:

```text
real camera NV12 frame
  -> split/read Y and UV layout
  -> derive Y, U, V planes
  -> warp Y into model view
  -> warp U into model view
  -> warp V into model view
  -> rejoin / pack YUV
  -> produce 6-channel model frame
  -> combine two frames into 12-channel input
```

## ONNX

ONNX is a model file format.

It stores a neural network graph in a framework-independent form:

```text
PyTorch / training framework
  -> export
  -> ONNX file
  -> inference runtime / compiler
```

An ONNX file contains:

```text
input names and shapes
layers / operators
weights
output names and shapes
graph structure
```

For an engineer analyzing a deployed ONNX model, the useful questions are:

1. What are the inputs?
2. What are the output tensors?
3. What preprocessing creates the inputs?
4. What postprocessing interprets the outputs?
5. Which parts are temporal?
6. Which outputs are directly used by controls?

The main warning:

```text
the ONNX graph alone is not the whole system
```

In OpenPilot, preprocessing and output parsing are equally important.

## Vision Encoder And Temporal Policy

The model can be mentally split into:

```text
vision encoder:
  turns camera tensors into learned visual features

temporal policy / recurrent part:
  uses current features plus memory/context to predict future outputs
```

The vision encoder answers:

```text
what is visually happening now?
```

The temporal policy answers:

```text
given current visual evidence and recent history,
what future motion / scene / action-relevant outputs make sense?
```

This is why inputs like `features_buffer`, `desire_pulse`, and `action_t` matter. The model is not stateless.

## `scene_feature`

`scene_feature` is a learned compact representation.

The practical mental model:

```text
raw image:
  huge, pixel-level information

scene_feature:
  compressed learned summary useful for the model's temporal reasoning
```

It is not a human-written semantic label like:

```text
"lane is curved"
```

It is a neural feature vector learned during training.

## Runtime: `ModelState`

`ModelState` is the object that owns the model runtime path.

Reference:

[ModelState class](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/modeld.py#L75)

It owns:

```text
compiled model runner
compiled warp function
image queues
feature buffers
hidden state / temporal state
input numpy buffers
output parser
```

Runtime tick:

```text
wrap camera buffer
create desire pulse
store traffic/action/context inputs
apply warp matrices
warp current frames
update image queues
run model
slice raw outputs
parse outputs
store hidden state for next tick
```

The key method:

[ModelState.run](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/modeld/modeld.py#L102)

## Output Parsing

The model emits a large raw output vector. That vector is not readable by itself.

The runtime must:

```text
slice output vector into named blocks
apply parser logic
convert logits into probabilities
decode mixture density outputs
fill model messages
```

Concepts covered:

```text
sigmoid:
  binary probability

softmax:
  category probability distribution

MDN:
  mixture density network output, useful for multi-modal prediction and uncertainty
```

The important idea:

```text
model output is structured after parsing,
not before parsing
```

## Plan To Action

The model predicts future motion/plan-like outputs. Downstream code extracts action-relevant quantities.

Important quantities:

```text
desiredAcceleration
desiredCurvature
shouldStop
```

Reference anchors:

1. [get_accel_from_plan](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/controls/lib/drive_helpers.py#L43)
2. [should_stop](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/controls/lib/drive_helpers.py#L56)
3. [get_curvature_from_plan](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/controls/lib/drive_helpers.py#L64)
4. [smooth_value](https://github.com/commaai/openpilot/blob/master/selfdrive/controls/lib/drive_helpers.py#L22)

The plan-to-action path:

```text
parsed plan
  -> desired acceleration
  -> should stop decision
  -> desired curvature
  -> smoothing
  -> action object
```

## Where The Model Stops

The model does not directly turn the steering motor.

The boundary is:

```text
model side:
  predicts future plan / desired motion

controls side:
  tracks desired motion using vehicle-specific controller logic
```

For lateral control:

```text
desired curvature / lateral target
  -> lateral controller
  -> steering-related command
```

For longitudinal control:

```text
desired acceleration / stop behavior
  -> longitudinal planner/controller
  -> acceleration/brake-related command
```

This boundary matters because the comma controls challenge sits below the vision model.

## How The Controls Challenge Connects

The comma controls challenge is:

[commaai/controls_challenge](https://github.com/commaai/controls_challenge)

The challenge is not about training OpenPilot's vision model.

It is about low-level control:

```text
given target lateral acceleration and current state,
choose steering action
so that the simulated car tracks the target smoothly
```

The challenge uses TinyPhysics, a learned/small simulator that predicts vehicle lateral acceleration response.

Important challenge objects:

```text
State
FuturePlan
TinyPhysicsModel
TinyPhysicsSimulator
BaseController
PID baseline controller
```

The challenge cost includes:

```text
lateral acceleration tracking cost
jerk / smoothness cost
```

The challenge is relevant because it is a small, measurable AV control environment where RL can be applied without needing to train the entire OpenPilot stack.

## Why We Deferred Controls Challenge Implementation

We started looking at controls challenge, but then paused it.

Reason:

```text
jumping straight to PPO or PufferLib would create another black box
```

The correct order is:

```text
core RL first
then PPO
then PufferLib
then controls challenge implementation
```

This is especially important because good RL engineering depends on problem formulation, not just code.

## Core RL Direction

The current learning target is core RL.

The core loop:

```text
state s_t
  -> policy chooses action a_t
  -> environment transitions
  -> reward r_t
  -> next state s_{t+1}
```

Compact notation:

```text
s_t -> pi(a_t | s_t) -> a_t
a_t -> environment -> s_{t+1}, r_t
```

The central difference from supervised learning:

```text
supervised learning:
  prediction is judged against a label

reinforcement learning:
  action changes the future, and reward may be delayed
```

That delayed consequence is why RL is hard.

## MDP

MDP means Markov Decision Process.

It defines:

```text
S:
  state space

A:
  action space

P:
  transition dynamics

R:
  reward function

gamma:
  discount factor
```

For the controls challenge:

```text
state:
  current vehicle/control values and future target info

action:
  steering command

transition:
  TinyPhysics predicts next lateral acceleration

reward:
  negative cost from tracking error and jerk

gamma:
  how much future smoothness/tracking matters
```

## Return

Return is accumulated future reward.

Without discounting:

```text
G_t = r_t + r_{t+1} + r_{t+2} + ...
```

With discounting:

```text
G_t = r_t + gamma r_{t+1} + gamma^2 r_{t+2} + ...
```

For driving control, future behavior matters. A steering action may look good immediately but cause oscillation later.

## Policy

The policy is the behavior rule.

It answers:

```text
given the current state, what action should I take?
```

For stochastic policies:

```text
pi(a | s) = probability of action a in state s
```

For continuous steering, a neural policy often outputs:

```text
mean action
standard deviation / exploration scale
```

During training, the agent samples actions. During evaluation, we often use the mean action.

## Value Function

The value function estimates expected future return.

```text
V(s) = expected future return starting from state s
```

Plain English:

```text
if I am in this state and keep following my policy,
how good is my future likely to be?
```

The value function is a critic, not the action itself.

## Advantage

Advantage asks whether an action was better or worse than expected.

```text
A(s, a) = Q(s, a) - V(s)
```

Plain English:

```text
was this action better than the usual action from this state?
```

PPO relies heavily on advantage estimates.

## Bellman Equation

Bellman thinking is:

```text
value now = reward now + discounted value later
```

Equation:

```text
V(s_t) = E[ r_t + gamma V(s_{t+1}) ]
```

This lets an agent learn from partial experience instead of waiting for the entire future every time.

## Why PPO Comes Later

PPO combines many concepts:

```text
stochastic policy
log probability
policy ratio
clipped objective
value loss
entropy bonus
advantage estimation
rollout buffer
on-policy update
```

If those concepts are not understood, PPO becomes a command-line ritual instead of an algorithm.

Correct learning order:

```text
MDP
  -> returns
  -> value functions
  -> Bellman equations
  -> Monte Carlo learning
  -> temporal difference learning
  -> policy gradients
  -> actor-critic
  -> GAE
  -> PPO
  -> PufferLib
  -> controls challenge
```

## PufferLib Role

PufferLib should be treated as a training systems tool.

It helps with:

```text
vectorized environments
fast rollout collection
agent/environment training loops
scaling experiments
```

It should not replace the RL mental model.

The correct mindset:

```text
understand the algorithm manually
then use PufferLib to run it efficiently
```

Reference:

[PufferLib documentation](https://puffer.ai/docs.html)

## Researcher Mindset

The goal is not just:

```text
make reward go up
```

The goal is:

```text
build a policy that improves real evaluation metrics
and understand why it works or fails
```

The working habits:

1. Define the MDP before writing the trainer.
2. Start with a baseline such as PID.
3. Reproduce the baseline locally.
4. Build the smallest environment wrapper first.
5. Overfit a tiny debug setting before scaling.
6. Separate training reward from evaluation cost.
7. Use deterministic evaluation.
8. Run multiple seeds.
9. Log failure cases.
10. Run ablations.
11. Watch for reward hacking.
12. Keep experiments reproducible.

The central question:

```text
did the learned policy improve the actual evaluation metric
without becoming brittle?
```
